case_data.title: DeBiasMe: Participatory AI Bias Mapping with K-12 Educators and Professionals
case_data.provide-a-brief-description-of-the-proje: DeBiasMe is a community-engaged AI literacy initiative that turns AI bias into learning contents publics can explore and act on together rather than a technical problem left to experts. Using an AI literacy toolkit of tangible "bias mapping" cards and cubes organised around four stages of the AI life cycle (prompt/input, data, model training, and output interpretation), DeBiasMe runs participatory workshops in which learners, educators or facilitators, and AI systems jointly examine where bias enters AI and who is responsible for addressing it. Run with K-12 teacher and professional cohorts in South Korea, with ongoing parallel pilots in the UK, the workshops surface how non-technical publics perceive and regulate AI bias and build their capacity to engage critically with it. The initiative connects grassroots engagement to a global standard: DeBiasMe supports the South Korea validation of the UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Students.
case_data.what-limitations-to-the-project-should-b:
1\. Convenience recruitment via partner networks likely skews toward educators and professionals already interested in AI.

2\. Sessions are facilitator-mediated; the full three-way learner–facilitator–AI dynamic has not yet been measured.
case_data.headline-findings: From "flaw to detect" to "responsibility to share." Non-experts could locate and name bias. Given the cards, teachers and professionals with no technical background could identify where bias enters (input / data / model / interpretation) and assign who should act on it. Participants reframed AI bias as a shared responsibility to regulate.
case_data.inclusion-efforts: The card/cube artifact requires no coding or technical background; it lets non-specialists locate and discuss bias through physical arrangement and conversation rather than jargon.
case_data.project-title: DeBiasMe: Participatory AI Bias Mapping with K-12 Educators and Professionals
case_data.why-is-this-project-important-to-include:
DeBiasMe brings into the casebook a set of voices and methods that are largely absent from the existing evidence base:
1. Communities rarely heard in AI governance: Participants are classroom teachers and non-technical professionals, people usually positioned only as end-users of AI. 
2. A novel, reusable participation method: The bias-mapping card and cube system is a low-tech, hands-on artifact that externalises the AI life cycle and makes an abstract concept ("bias") concrete, locatable, and negotiable across a group. It is designed to be reused by other facilitators.
3. Our project reframes the unit of engagement: Rather than asking individuals to detect bias, the workshop distributes the work of scrutinising AI across people, making bias a collective and deliberative learning object. 
4. It builds power, not just data. The aim is to leave participants more able to question and shape AI in their own settings, and to connect that capacity to a global policy instrument (UNESCO AI CFS).
project-goals: Methods: Create re-usable participation tools & methods
Quantitative: Generate statistical evidence on public attitudes to AI
Qualitative: Capture qualitative evidence on public attitudes to AI
Capacity: Build participant capacity to engage with AI
Audit: Review design or implementation of AI tools
Empowerment: Build community power with respect to AI
Evaluate: Check the quality of evidence or engagement processes
case_data.describe-the-subject-matter-in-your-own-: How AI and human bias emerges across AI life cycle, and how educators, learners, and professionals can collectively recognize and regulate it.
